Front:
A new team member asks how Git and GitHub differ. Which statement most accurately describes the relationship?

A) Git is a distributed version control system, while GitHub is a cloud platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features
B) Git and GitHub are two competing version control systems, and a project must choose exactly one of them to track history
C) GitHub is the command-line tool that records commits, while Git is the website used to review and merge those commits online
Back:
A) Git is a distributed version control system, while GitHub is a cloud platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features

Git is the underlying VCS created by Linus Torvalds; GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform built around Git.

Reference: About GitHub and Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: Remember: Git works fully offline on your machine; GitHub adds pull requests, issues, Actions, and access control on top of Git. You can use Git without GitHub, but not the reverse.

Front:
Why is Git described as a 'distributed' version control system rather than a centralized one?

A) All history lives only on a central server, so developers must stay connected to commit any change to the project
B) Every clone contains the full project history, so developers can commit and view history locally without a network connection
C) The repository is split into fragments across many servers, and no single machine ever holds the complete commit history
Back:
B) Every clone contains the full project history, so developers can commit and view history locally without a network connection

In Git, each clone is a complete repository with full history, enabling offline work and resilience.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: Contrast with centralized systems like SVN where history lives on one server. Distributed history means no single point of failure and fast local operations.

Front:
A developer wants a local working copy of a remote GitHub repository, including its full commit history. Which Git command should they use?

A) git init, which starts tracking the current empty folder as a brand-new local repository with no linked remote history
B) git pull, which updates an already-existing local repository with the newest commits from its configured upstream remote
C) git clone
Back:
C) git clone

git clone downloads a full copy of a remote repository, including all history, and configures the remote automatically.

Reference: Cloning a repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: git init creates a new empty repo; git pull only works after a repo already exists locally. Use clone once to get started, then pull to stay updated.

Front:
In Git, what is the purpose of the staging area (the index) when using git add?

A) It permanently writes the selected changes into project history and immediately publishes them to the remote repository
B) It lets you select exactly which changes will be included in the next commit before you actually record that commit
C) It creates a separate branch automatically so unfinished changes never affect the current branch you are on
Back:
B) It lets you select exactly which changes will be included in the next commit before you actually record that commit

The staging area holds the snapshot of changes that git commit will record, giving fine-grained control over commit contents.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: Workflow: edit files, git add to stage, git commit to record. Staging lets you split unrelated changes into separate, meaningful commits.

Front:
What does a Git commit represent within a repository?

A) A saved snapshot of staged changes at a point in time, along with author, message, and a link to previous commits
B) A temporary draft of edits stored only in memory that disappears the moment the editor or terminal window is closed
C) A request asking a project maintainer to review and combine one branch into another branch on GitHub
Back:
A) A saved snapshot of staged changes at a point in time, along with author, message, and a link to previous commits

Each commit records a snapshot plus metadata and references its parent, forming the project history.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: A commit is immutable and identified by a SHA hash. The 'request to combine branches' description is a pull request, not a commit.

Front:
A developer wants to work on a new feature without affecting the stable code. What is the recommended Git approach?

A) Copy the entire project into a second folder and manually merge the edited files back one at a time when finished
B) Edit files directly on the main branch but avoid committing until the feature is completely finished and tested
C) Create a new branch, make commits there, and later merge it back into the main branch
Back:
C) Create a new branch, make commits there, and later merge it back into the main branch

Branches isolate work so the main line stays stable; changes merge back when ready, typically via a pull request.

Reference: GitHub flow - GitHub Docs
Extra: Branching is lightweight in Git. This is the foundation of GitHub flow: branch, commit, open a PR, review, merge.

Front:
After committing changes locally, which command uploads those commits to the corresponding branch on GitHub?

A) git commit, which finalizes the staged changes into local history but does not send anything to the remote repository
B) git push
C) git fetch, which downloads new commits and refs from the remote but does not upload any of your local commits
Back:
B) git push

git push transfers local commits on a branch to the matching branch on the remote (GitHub).

Reference: Pushing commits to a remote repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: commit records locally; push publishes. fetch is the opposite direction (download only). Push regularly so collaborators can see your work.

Front:
What is the key difference between git fetch and git pull?

A) git fetch downloads remote changes without merging them, while git pull downloads and then merges them into your current branch
B) git fetch permanently overwrites your local commits with the remote version, while git pull safely keeps a backup of your local work first
C) git fetch works only on private repositories, while git pull is required for any repository that has been made public on GitHub
Back:
A) git fetch downloads remote changes without merging them, while git pull downloads and then merges them into your current branch

git pull is effectively git fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into the current branch.

Reference: Getting changes from a remote repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: Use fetch to inspect incoming changes before integrating; use pull when you want to update your branch immediately. Neither depends on repo visibility.

Front:
Which sequence best describes the GitHub flow for proposing a change?

A) Push directly to main, then notify teammates by email so they can review the change after it is already live in production
B) Create a branch, commit changes, open a pull request, review and discuss, then merge into the default branch
C) Fork the repository, delete the default branch, and rebuild the project history from scratch before submitting changes
Back:
B) Create a branch, commit changes, open a pull request, review and discuss, then merge into the default branch

GitHub flow is a lightweight, branch-based workflow centered on pull requests for review before merging.

Reference: GitHub flow - GitHub Docs
Extra: GitHub flow keeps main deployable at all times. The pull request is the collaboration hub for review, discussion, and automated checks.

Front:
In a cloned repository, what does the remote named 'origin' typically refer to?

A) The local .git folder on your computer where all staged changes are temporarily written before they become commits
B) The default alias pointing to the remote repository the project was cloned from, such as its GitHub URL
C) A protected branch that only repository administrators are allowed to push commits to after passing status checks
Back:
B) The default alias pointing to the remote repository the project was cloned from, such as its GitHub URL

By convention, git clone names the source remote 'origin', which you push to and fetch from.

Reference: Managing remote repositories - GitHub Docs
Extra: origin is just a convenient name; you can add other remotes (e.g., 'upstream' when working from a fork). It is not a branch.

Front:
Which lightweight markup language does GitHub use to format README files, issues, and comments?

A) Markdown
B) A proprietary binary formatting format that can only be edited using GitHub's own desktop application on Windows
C) HTML exclusively, meaning plain text and shorthand formatting symbols are stripped out and never rendered on GitHub
Back:
A) Markdown

GitHub uses GitHub Flavored Markdown to render formatted text in READMEs, issues, PRs, and comments.

Reference: Basic writing and formatting syntax - GitHub Docs
Extra: GitHub supports limited HTML inside Markdown, plus extensions like task lists, tables, and @mentions. Markdown files use the .md extension.

Front:
How is a GitHub repository best described?

A) A single immutable text file that stores only the latest version of a project's source code and nothing else
B) A user's public profile page that summarizes their contribution activity across all projects on the platform
C) A container for a project's files and their complete version history, plus settings, issues, and pull requests
Back:
C) A container for a project's files and their complete version history, plus settings, issues, and pull requests

A repository holds project files, full history, and collaboration features such as issues and pull requests.

Reference: About repositories - GitHub Docs
Extra: A repo is the fundamental unit on GitHub. It can belong to a personal account or an organization and can be public, private, or internal.

Front:
What is a key difference between a personal account and an organization account on GitHub?

A) Personal accounts can host code, but organization accounts are limited to hosting documentation and project boards only
B) An organization is a shared account for group collaboration with teams and centralized permissions, while a personal account represents one individual
C) Only personal accounts can create private repositories, whereas organization accounts are restricted to public repositories exclusively
Back:
B) An organization is a shared account for group collaboration with teams and centralized permissions, while a personal account represents one individual

Organizations enable many users to collaborate with teams, roles, and centralized administration.

Reference: About organizations - GitHub Docs
Extra: Organizations own repositories collectively and support teams for scalable access management. Both account types can host public and private repos.

Front:
A developer wants to contribute to an open-source project where they lack write access. What is the standard first step?

A) Fork the repository to create their own copy, then make changes and open a pull request back to the original
B) Request that a maintainer grant them administrator rights on the project so they can push commits directly to main
C) Clone the repository locally and force-push their new commits over the project's default branch when finished
Back:
A) Fork the repository to create their own copy, then make changes and open a pull request back to the original

Forking creates a personal server-side copy; contributors work there and propose changes via pull requests.

Reference: Contributing to a project - GitHub Docs
Extra: The fork-and-pull model is the backbone of open-source contribution. You never need write access to the original repo to propose changes.

Front:
In Git, what does HEAD normally point to?

A) The oldest commit in the repository, which serves as the permanent anchor that all later branches ultimately descend from
B) The remote tracking reference that always reflects the exact current state of the branch stored on the GitHub server
C) The current branch or commit you have checked out, indicating your present position in the repository history
Back:
C) The current branch or commit you have checked out, indicating your present position in the repository history

HEAD is a pointer to the currently checked-out branch tip (or commit), marking where new commits attach.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: When you switch branches with git checkout/switch, HEAD moves to point at the new branch. A 'detached HEAD' points directly at a commit instead of a branch.

Front:
Two developers edited the same lines of the same file on different branches. When merging, what happens?

A) Git silently discards one developer's changes and keeps only the most recently committed version without any warning
B) Git reports a merge conflict that a person must resolve by choosing or combining the conflicting changes
C) Git automatically emails both developers and locks the repository until an administrator manually approves the merge
Back:
B) Git reports a merge conflict that a person must resolve by choosing or combining the conflicting changes

When the same lines change on both sides, Git cannot auto-merge and marks a conflict for manual resolution.

Reference: About merge conflicts - GitHub Docs
Extra: Git auto-merges non-overlapping changes. Conflicts require human judgment because Git cannot know which version is correct. Communicate to reduce them.

Front:
Which practice makes commit history most useful to a team?

A) Writing clear, concise commit messages that explain what changed and why for each logical change
B) Committing all changes for an entire release in a single large commit at the very end to keep the log short
C) Reusing the same generic message such as 'update' for every commit so the history stays visually consistent
Back:
A) Writing clear, concise commit messages that explain what changed and why for each logical change

Descriptive messages and small logical commits make history readable, reviewable, and easy to debug.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: Good history helps with git blame, reverts, and code review. Prefer small, focused commits over one giant commit or vague repeated messages.

Front:
What is stored in the hidden .git directory inside a Git repository?

A) Only a plain-text backup copy of the most recent version of each tracked file, without any earlier historical versions
B) The remote server credentials and personal access tokens required to authenticate every push to GitHub
C) The repository's complete object database and metadata, including all commits, branches, and configuration
Back:
C) The repository's complete object database and metadata, including all commits, branches, and configuration

The .git directory contains everything Git needs: objects, refs, config, and history that make the folder a repository.

Reference: About Git - GitHub Docs
Extra: Deleting .git turns the folder back into ordinary files with no history. Credentials are typically stored by a separate credential helper, not in .git objects.

Front:
An organization wants a repository that is visible to all enterprise members but hidden from the public internet. Which visibility setting fits?

A) Public visibility, which exposes the repository and its code to anyone on the internet, including non-members
B) Private visibility, which limits access strictly to individually invited collaborators and nobody else in the enterprise
C) Internal visibility, which makes the repository readable by all enterprise members while keeping it hidden from the public
Back:
C) Internal visibility, which makes the repository readable by all enterprise members while keeping it hidden from the public

Internal repositories are visible to all members of the enterprise but not to the public, ideal for InnerSource.

Reference: About repositories - GitHub Docs
Extra: Internal visibility requires GitHub Enterprise. It enables InnerSource: sharing across the whole org while staying hidden from outside the enterprise.

Front:
What is the primary purpose of a repository's README file?

A) It lists every user who has ever been granted administrator access to the repository over its entire lifetime
B) It communicates what the project does and how to use it, and is displayed on the repository home page
C) It defines which files and folders Git should ignore so they are never tracked or committed to the repository
Back:
B) It communicates what the project does and how to use it, and is displayed on the repository home page

The README introduces the project and renders automatically on the repository landing page.

Reference: About READMEs - GitHub Docs
Extra: A profile README (in a repo named after your username) shows on your GitHub profile. The file that lists ignored paths is .gitignore, not the README.

Front:
What does a .gitignore file do in a repository?

A) It specifies intentionally untracked files and patterns that Git should not stage or commit
B) It records the license terms that govern how others may reuse and distribute the project's source code
C) It stores a prioritized list of open issues so that contributors know which tasks to work on first
Back:
A) It specifies intentionally untracked files and patterns that Git should not stage or commit

.gitignore lists paths and patterns (like build output or secrets) that Git should exclude from tracking.

Reference: Ignoring files - GitHub Docs
Extra: Already-tracked files are not affected by adding them to .gitignore; you must untrack them first. GitHub offers language-specific templates when creating a repo.

Front:
Why is adding a LICENSE file important for a public open-source repository?

A) Without a license file, GitHub will automatically delete the repository after a fixed grace period of inactivity
B) A license file is required by Git before any commits can be pushed to a repository that has been made public
C) It defines the legal terms under which others may use, modify, and distribute the code
Back:
C) It defines the legal terms under which others may use, modify, and distribute the code

Without a license, default copyright applies and others generally have no rights to reuse the code.

Reference: Licensing a repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: No license means 'all rights reserved' by default. GitHub can suggest common licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL) when you create or add one via the web UI.

Front:
A team wants to package a specific version of their software with binaries and release notes for users to download. Which GitHub feature should they use?

A) Releases, which are based on Git tags and can include notes and downloadable release assets
B) Gists, which are standalone snippet documents intended for sharing small pieces of code outside a repository
C) The repository wiki, which provides free-form documentation pages but does not attach versioned binary downloads
Back:
A) Releases, which are based on Git tags and can include notes and downloadable release assets

Releases build on tags to publish versioned deliverables, release notes, and attached binaries.

Reference: About releases - GitHub Docs
Extra: A tag marks a point in history; a release adds a user-facing package around that tag. Gists and wikis do not provide versioned binary distribution.

Front:
What is a GitHub Gist primarily used for?

A) Hosting and running continuous integration workflows that build and test a full application on every push
B) Sharing small snippets of code or notes, either publicly or secretly, with optional version history
C) Storing large binary media assets such as videos and datasets that exceed normal repository size limits
Back:
B) Sharing small snippets of code or notes, either publicly or secretly, with optional version history

Gists are lightweight, shareable snippets that are themselves Git repositories, available as public or secret.

Reference: Creating gists - GitHub Docs
Extra: Secret gists are not searchable but are still accessible to anyone with the URL. Gists suit quick shares; full projects belong in repositories.

Front:
An organization repeatedly creates repositories with the same starter files and structure. Which feature reduces this repetitive setup?

A) A template repository, which lets users generate new repositories preloaded with the same starting files and structure
B) A repository fork, which links a full copy back to the source for the purpose of contributing changes upstream
C) A protected branch rule, which enforces reviews and status checks before code can be merged into main
Back:
A) A template repository, which lets users generate new repositories preloaded with the same starting files and structure

Marking a repo as a template lets others create fresh, unlinked repos seeded with its contents.

Reference: Creating a template repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: Unlike a fork, a repo generated from a template has no shared commit history and no link back to the source, giving a clean starting point.

Front:
Where can a maintainer view traffic, clones, and contributor activity for a repository?

A) In the Actions tab, which is dedicated to running and reviewing automated workflow executions and their logs
B) In the repository's Insights tab, which shows analytics such as traffic, contributors, and dependency data
C) In the Security tab, which surfaces vulnerability alerts and code scanning results rather than usage statistics
Back:
B) In the repository's Insights tab, which shows analytics such as traffic, contributors, and dependency data

The Insights tab aggregates repository analytics including traffic, commits, contributors, and dependencies.

Reference: Viewing traffic to a repository - GitHub Docs
Extra: Insights also includes the community standards checklist and the dependency graph. Actions shows workflow runs; Security shows alerts.

Front:
What is the role of the default branch in a GitHub repository?

A) It is a read-only archival branch that stores historical releases and cannot receive any new commits after creation
B) It is the base branch shown by default and the target for new pull requests and clones, commonly named main
C) It is a hidden branch used exclusively by GitHub Actions to store workflow logs and temporary build artifacts
Back:
B) It is the base branch shown by default and the target for new pull requests and clones, commonly named main

The default branch is the primary branch presented to users and the default base for PRs and clones.

Reference: Changing the default branch - GitHub Docs
Extra: Historically 'master', the default branch is now typically 'main'. You can rename or change which branch is default in repository settings.

Front:
A team wants specific people automatically requested for review whenever certain files change. Which file enables this?

A) The CONTRIBUTING.md file, which explains contribution guidelines but does not assign reviewers to any pull request
B) The CODEOWNERS file, which maps file paths to owners who are automatically requested to review matching changes
C) The SECURITY.md file, which documents how to report vulnerabilities but plays no role in review assignment
Back:
B) The CODEOWNERS file, which maps file paths to owners who are automatically requested to review matching changes

CODEOWNERS defines owners per path; matching pull requests automatically request those reviewers.

Reference: About code owners - GitHub Docs
Extra: Combined with branch protection, code owner review can be made mandatory. CONTRIBUTING and SECURITY guide contributors but do not assign reviewers.

Front:
How can a user make a repository easier to discover by categorizing it around subjects like 'machine-learning' or 'cli'?

A) By adding repository topics, which are labels that categorize repositories and improve discoverability in search
B) By renaming the default branch to match the subject so that search engines index the repository more effectively
C) By creating an issue for each subject area and pinning those issues to the top of the repository's issue list
Back:
A) By adding repository topics, which are labels that categorize repositories and improve discoverability in search

Topics are searchable tags added to a repository to describe its purpose, language, or domain.

Reference: Classifying your repository with topics - GitHub Docs
Extra: Topics power exploration at github.com/topics. They differ from issue labels, which categorize issues and PRs within a single repository.

Front:
What is the difference between starring and watching a repository on GitHub?

A) Starring subscribes you to every notification, while watching simply adds the repository to a private read-only list
B) Starring bookmarks a repository and shows appreciation, while watching subscribes you to its activity notifications
C) Starring grants you write access to the repository, while watching grants you read-only access to its source code
Back:
B) Starring bookmarks a repository and shows appreciation, while watching subscribes you to its activity notifications

Stars are bookmarks/signals of interest; watching controls your notification subscription for repo activity.

Reference: Saving repositories with stars - GitHub Docs
Extra: Neither starring nor watching changes access permissions. Watching can be customized to all activity, participating only, or specific event types.

Front:
A project is no longer maintained but the team wants to keep it read-only and clearly signal its status. What should they do?

A) Delete the repository so it disappears entirely, then recreate it later if anyone ever needs the code again
B) Change the repository visibility to private so that only the original maintainers can continue to view the code
C) Archive the repository, which makes it read-only and clearly marks it as no longer actively maintained
Back:
C) Archive the repository, which makes it read-only and clearly marks it as no longer actively maintained

Archiving preserves the repo in a read-only state and displays a banner indicating it is no longer maintained.

Reference: Archiving repositories - GitHub Docs
Extra: Archived repos can still be viewed, cloned, and starred but not modified. You can unarchive later. Deleting loses history and links; visibility is unrelated.

Front:
A developer wants to host a free static website directly from files in a GitHub repository. Which feature provides this?

A) GitHub Pages, which publishes a static website hosted directly from a branch or folder in the repository
B) GitHub Codespaces, which provisions a cloud development environment for editing and running code in the browser
C) GitHub Packages, which hosts and distributes software packages and container images tied to the repository
Back:
A) GitHub Pages, which publishes a static website hosted directly from a branch or folder in the repository

GitHub Pages serves static sites straight from a repository branch or /docs folder, optionally built with Jekyll.

Reference: About GitHub Pages - GitHub Docs
Extra: Pages is for static content (HTML/CSS/JS). Codespaces is a dev environment, and Packages is a package registry, neither of which hosts a public website.

Front:
Which GitHub search qualifier restricts a code search to results within a single repository?

A) The user: qualifier, which narrows results to every repository owned by a specified account across the platform
B) The repo:owner/name qualifier, which limits the search to code inside that one specific repository
C) The language: qualifier, which filters by programming language but does not confine results to any one repository
Back:
B) The repo:owner/name qualifier, which limits the search to code inside that one specific repository

The repo: qualifier scopes searches to a specific repository by owner and name.

Reference: Searching code - GitHub Docs
Extra: Combine qualifiers to refine results, e.g., repo:owner/name language:python. user: broadens to an account; language: filters by language across many repos.

Front:
A maintainer wants to know who last changed a specific line of code and in which commit. Which feature helps?

A) The blame view, which annotates each line of a file with the commit and author that last modified it
B) The releases page, which lists tagged versions and notes but does not attribute individual lines of code
C) The dependency graph, which shows external libraries the project relies on rather than authorship of lines
Back:
A) The blame view, which annotates each line of a file with the commit and author that last modified it

Git blame maps each line to the commit that last changed it, aiding investigation and code archaeology.

Reference: Viewing a file - GitHub Docs
Extra: Blame is great for understanding why a line exists. From a blame line you can jump to the commit and its pull request for full context.

Front:
What is the key difference between forking a repository and cloning it?

A) Forking downloads the repository onto your computer, while cloning creates a server-side copy under your account on GitHub
B) Forking permanently transfers ownership of the original repository, while cloning simply grants you temporary read access to it
C) Forking creates a linked server-side copy under your account on GitHub, while cloning downloads a repository to your local machine
Back:
C) Forking creates a linked server-side copy under your account on GitHub, while cloning downloads a repository to your local machine

A fork is a server-side copy on GitHub linked to the original; a clone is a local download of a repository.

Reference: About forks - GitHub Docs
Extra: A common flow combines both: fork on GitHub, then clone your fork locally. Forking does not transfer ownership; the original repo is unaffected.

Front:
Where does GitHub look for community health files like CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md if they are not in a specific repository?

A) In a repository named .github owned by the same account or organization, which provides default community health files
B) In the repository's releases page, where GitHub stores fallback documentation that applies when no other files are present
C) In the account's public profile README, which GitHub reuses as the default contributing guide for every repository
Back:
A) In a repository named .github owned by the same account or organization, which provides default community health files

Default community health files placed in a special .github repository apply to all repos owned by that account or org that lack their own.

Reference: Creating a default community health file - GitHub Docs
Extra: This centralizes CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, and issue templates across many repos. A repo's own files always override the defaults.

Front:
What is the primary purpose of a GitHub issue?

A) To automatically deploy the latest version of an application to production whenever the default branch is updated
B) To track a task, bug, enhancement, or question and enable discussion and assignment within a repository
C) To store the compiled build artifacts and binaries that result from a successful continuous integration run
Back:
B) To track a task, bug, enhancement, or question and enable discussion and assignment within a repository

Issues track work items and discussions, supporting labels, assignees, milestones, and references.

Reference: About issues - GitHub Docs
Extra: Issues are the unit of planning and collaboration. They can be linked to pull requests and organized on GitHub Projects boards.

Front:
How are labels used within a repository's issues and pull requests?

A) They restrict which collaborators are permitted to comment on or close a given issue or pull request thread
B) They categorize and filter issues and pull requests, for example 'bug', 'documentation', or 'good first issue'
C) They automatically merge a pull request as soon as all required status checks have finished passing on it
Back:
B) They categorize and filter issues and pull requests, for example 'bug', 'documentation', or 'good first issue'

Labels tag issues and PRs for classification and filtering; they do not control permissions or merging.

Reference: Managing labels - GitHub Docs
Extra: Labels are repo-scoped and color-coded. 'good first issue' helps newcomers find approachable tasks. They organize work but grant no access.

Front:
A team wants to group issues and pull requests toward a target release with a due date and progress tracking. Which feature fits?

A) Milestones, which group issues and pull requests toward a goal and track completion progress and a due date
B) Reactions, which let users add emoji responses to comments to express agreement without adding extra noise
C) Saved replies, which store reusable text so maintainers can respond to common questions more quickly
Back:
A) Milestones, which group issues and pull requests toward a goal and track completion progress and a due date

Milestones bundle related issues/PRs toward a release goal and show a progress bar and optional due date.

Reference: About milestones - GitHub Docs
Extra: Milestones are ideal for sprint or release tracking. Labels categorize; milestones measure progress toward a dated goal.

Front:
What does assigning a user to an issue accomplish?

A) It grants that user administrator permissions on the repository so they can change settings and manage other members
B) It automatically closes the issue and records the assigned user as the person who resolved the underlying problem
C) It indicates who is responsible for working on the issue, making ownership visible to the whole team
Back:
C) It indicates who is responsible for working on the issue, making ownership visible to the whole team

Assignees show who owns an issue or pull request; it does not change permissions or status.

Reference: Assigning issues and pull requests - GitHub Docs
Extra: Multiple assignees are allowed. Assignment clarifies responsibility but does not alter access rights or automatically close anything.

Front:
What is the core function of a pull request on GitHub?

A) To propose merging changes from one branch into another, enabling review, discussion, and automated checks first
B) To permanently delete a feature branch after its work is complete without allowing any review of the changes
C) To download the latest changes from a remote repository into the developer's local working copy of the code
Back:
A) To propose merging changes from one branch into another, enabling review, discussion, and automated checks first

A pull request proposes changes for review before merging, integrating discussion and status checks.

Reference: About pull requests - GitHub Docs
Extra: PRs are the heart of collaboration on GitHub. Downloading remote changes is git pull; deleting a branch is a separate cleanup step after merge.

Front:
When should a developer open a draft pull request?

A) When they want the pull request to bypass all required status checks and merge instantly without any review
B) When work is still in progress and they want feedback but signal that it is not yet ready to merge
C) When they need to permanently archive an abandoned branch so that it can never be reopened or merged later
Back:
B) When work is still in progress and they want feedback but signal that it is not yet ready to merge

Draft PRs mark work as not ready to merge; they cannot be merged until marked ready for review.

Reference: About pull requests - GitHub Docs
Extra: Drafts still run CI and allow comments but block merging and (optionally) code owner requests until you click 'Ready for review'.

Front:
During a pull request review, which three outcomes can a reviewer submit?

A) Approve, request changes, or comment
B) Merge immediately, delete the source branch, or permanently lock the entire conversation from further replies
C) Assign a milestone, add a label, or convert the pull request back into a plain issue for later triage
Back:
A) Approve, request changes, or comment

A review can approve the changes, request changes (blocking), or leave general comments.

Reference: About pull request reviews - GitHub Docs
Extra: 'Request changes' can block merging when required. Comment leaves feedback without an explicit approval or block. These are review verdicts, not merge actions.

Front:
A repository requires at least two approving reviews before merging. Which mechanism enforces this?

A) A repository label named 'needs-review' that maintainers must manually remove before the merge button becomes active
B) A milestone due date that automatically prevents merging until the configured target release date has passed
C) A branch protection rule that requires a set number of approving pull request reviews before merging
Back:
C) A branch protection rule that requires a set number of approving pull request reviews before merging

Branch protection rules can require approvals, status checks, and other conditions before a merge is allowed.

Reference: About protected branches - GitHub Docs
Extra: Branch protection can also require passing checks, code owner review, and up-to-date branches. Labels and milestones do not enforce merge rules.

Front:
How do GitHub Discussions differ from issues?

A) Discussions run automated CI pipelines, whereas issues are limited to storing static text and screenshots only
B) Discussions provide a forum for open-ended conversation and Q&A, while issues track actionable work items
C) Discussions are private to repository administrators, while issues are always visible to the entire public internet
Back:
B) Discussions provide a forum for open-ended conversation and Q&A, while issues track actionable work items

Discussions suit community questions, ideas, and announcements; issues track concrete, trackable tasks.

Reference: About discussions - GitHub Docs
Extra: Discussions support Q&A with marked answers, categories, and upvotes. Convert a discussion to an issue when it becomes actionable work.

Front:
A developer writes 'Closes #42' in a pull request description. What happens when the PR merges into the default branch?

A) Issue #42 is automatically closed and linked to the pull request that resolved it
B) The text is treated as a plain string, and issue #42 must still be closed manually by a maintainer afterward
C) A brand-new issue numbered 42 is created and immediately assigned to whoever authored the pull request
Back:
A) Issue #42 is automatically closed and linked to the pull request that resolved it

Keywords like 'closes', 'fixes', or 'resolves' followed by an issue reference auto-close the issue on merge.

Reference: Linking a pull request to an issue - GitHub Docs
Extra: This only closes the issue when merged into the default branch. Supported keywords include close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves, resolved.

Front:
What is the effect of typing @username in an issue or pull request comment?

A) It permanently assigns that user as the sole person responsible for resolving the issue or pull request
B) It mentions and notifies that user, drawing their attention to the comment or thread
C) It grants that user temporary write access to the repository so they can push commits to the branch
Back:
B) It mentions and notifies that user, drawing their attention to the comment or thread

@mentions notify the referenced user (or team) so they are alerted to the conversation.

Reference: Basic writing and formatting syntax - GitHub Docs
Extra: You can @mention teams too. Mentioning notifies but does not assign or grant access; those are separate actions.

Front:
Typing #123 in an issue comment creates what?

A) A cross-reference link to issue or pull request number 123 in the same repository
B) A new label named 123 that is instantly applied to the current issue for later filtering
C) A commit whose message is the number 123, recorded against the repository's default branch
Back:
A) A cross-reference link to issue or pull request number 123 in the same repository

The #number syntax auto-links to the referenced issue or PR, building a web of related work.

Reference: Autolinked references and URLs - GitHub Docs
Extra: Cross-references appear as timeline events on the referenced item, helping trace relationships between issues and pull requests.

Front:
How do task lists in a Markdown issue body help track progress?

A) They render interactive checkboxes whose completion percentage is shown on the issue and in project views
B) They automatically assign each checkbox item to a different collaborator based on repository write permissions
C) They convert each unchecked item into a separate new issue as soon as the issue body is first saved
Back:
A) They render interactive checkboxes whose completion percentage is shown on the issue and in project views

Task list items with - [ ] and - [x] render as clickable checkboxes and show completion progress.

Reference: About task lists - GitHub Docs
Extra: Checking a box updates the issue in real time. Task lists are a lightweight way to break work into trackable sub-steps within one issue.

Front:
A user wants to control which repository events send them updates. Which feature governs this?

A) Repository forks, which create independent copies but do not influence which events send the user updates
B) Notification subscriptions and watch settings, which determine which repository events generate updates for the user
C) Pull request reviews, which record approvals or change requests but do not manage a user's update preferences
Back:
B) Notification subscriptions and watch settings, which determine which repository events generate updates for the user

Watching and subscription settings control which events (issues, PRs, releases) trigger notifications.

Reference: About notifications - GitHub Docs
Extra: You can watch all activity, participating-and-mentions only, or custom event types. Notifications arrive in the inbox and optionally by email.

Front:
A maintainer frequently types the same response to duplicate issues. Which feature speeds this up?

A) Saved replies, which store reusable comment text that can be inserted into issue and pull request responses
B) Milestones, which group related issues toward a release but do not store any reusable response text
C) Branch protection, which enforces review rules on merges and is unrelated to composing repeated comments
Back:
A) Saved replies, which store reusable comment text that can be inserted into issue and pull request responses

Saved replies let you store and quickly insert commonly used responses in issues and PRs.

Reference: About saved replies - GitHub Docs
Extra: Saved replies are account-level, so they work across all your repositories. They cut repetitive typing for triage and support.

Front:
With a CODEOWNERS file configured, what happens when a pull request modifies an owned path?

A) The pull request is blocked from opening entirely until every listed code owner has already left an approving review
B) The listed code owners are automatically requested as reviewers for that pull request
C) The pull request is merged automatically as soon as continuous integration checks finish, skipping human review
Back:
B) The listed code owners are automatically requested as reviewers for that pull request

When a PR touches an owned path, GitHub automatically requests review from the matching code owners.

Reference: About code owners - GitHub Docs
Extra: With branch protection, code owner approval can be made required. By itself, CODEOWNERS requests reviewers but does not block opening or auto-merge.

Front:
A contributor forked a repository, made changes, and now wants them considered for the original project. What do they do?

A) Open a pull request from their fork's branch to the original repository's branch for the maintainers to review
B) Send the maintainers a downloadable ZIP archive of their fork so the maintainers can copy the files in manually
C) Push their fork's branch directly onto the original repository's default branch using their existing read access
Back:
A) Open a pull request from their fork's branch to the original repository's branch for the maintainers to review

Cross-fork pull requests let contributors propose changes from their fork to the upstream repository.

Reference: Creating a pull request from a fork - GitHub Docs
Extra: Read access does not permit pushing to the upstream default branch. The fork-and-PR model is how external contributors participate in open source.

Front:
What is a GitHub repository wiki intended for?

A) Running scheduled automation jobs that build, test, and deploy the project on a recurring nightly basis
B) Hosting long-form documentation such as guides and references in editable, version-controlled pages
C) Storing encrypted secrets and API keys that continuous integration workflows read during a build
Back:
B) Hosting long-form documentation such as guides and references in editable, version-controlled pages

Wikis provide collaborative, versioned documentation pages separate from the main codebase.

Reference: About wikis - GitHub Docs
Extra: Wikis are themselves Git repositories. For docs versioned with code, many teams prefer a /docs folder or GitHub Pages instead.

Front:
A reviewer wants to see the exact line-by-line differences between two branches before opening a pull request. Which feature helps?

A) The compare view, which shows the commits and diff between two branches, tags, or commits
B) The Insights traffic graph, which reports clones and visitors but does not display code differences between branches
C) The releases page, which lists published versions and notes rather than a line-by-line comparison of branches
Back:
A) The compare view, which shows the commits and diff between two branches, tags, or commits

The compare view displays commits and a unified diff between any two refs, useful before creating a PR.

Reference: Comparing commits - GitHub Docs
Extra: You can even compare across forks. Opening a PR is essentially formalizing a compare view for review and merge.

Front:
What is the purpose of emoji reactions on issues, pull requests, and comments?

A) They let users quickly express agreement or sentiment without adding another full comment to the thread
B) They automatically escalate the item to repository administrators once a threshold number of reactions is reached
C) They lock the comment so that no further edits or replies can be added by anyone in the conversation
Back:
A) They let users quickly express agreement or sentiment without adding another full comment to the thread

Reactions provide lightweight feedback (like thumbs up) and reduce '+1' comment noise.

Reference: Reactions - GitHub Docs
Extra: Reactions can help gauge community interest in feature requests without cluttering the discussion with duplicate comments.

Front:
When merging a pull request, which merge method combines all of the branch's commits into a single new commit on the base branch?

A) The squash and merge option, which condenses all commits from the pull request into one commit on the base branch
B) The rebase and merge option, which replays each individual commit from the branch onto the tip of the base branch
C) The create a merge commit option, which preserves every branch commit and adds one extra merge commit joining them
Back:
A) The squash and merge option, which condenses all commits from the pull request into one commit on the base branch

Squash and merge collapses all PR commits into one, producing a clean, linear base history.

Reference: About pull request merges - GitHub Docs
Extra: Merge commit preserves full history with a merge node; rebase replays commits without a merge commit; squash yields one tidy commit. Choose per team convention.

Front:
A maintainer wants two or three key issues to appear at the top of the repository's issue list. Which feature accomplishes this?

A) Pinning the issues, which displays a limited number of selected issues at the top of the issues list
B) Adding a 'pinned' label, which changes the color of the selected issues but does not reorder the issues list
C) Assigning the issues to a milestone, which groups them by release but does not move them to the top of the list
Back:
A) Pinning the issues, which displays a limited number of selected issues at the top of the issues list

Pinned issues surface important items (like FAQs or roadmaps) at the top of the issues tab.

Reference: Pinning an issue - GitHub Docs
Extra: You can pin up to three issues per repository. Labels categorize and milestones group by goal, but neither reorders the list to the top.

Front:
How do issue templates improve bug reporting in a repository?

A) They automatically resolve reported bugs by generating a code fix and opening a pull request for the maintainer
B) They prompt reporters with a predefined structure so submitted issues include the information maintainers need
C) They restrict issue creation to repository administrators so that only trusted maintainers can file new reports
Back:
B) They prompt reporters with a predefined structure so submitted issues include the information maintainers need

Issue templates and forms standardize submissions, guiding reporters to include necessary details.

Reference: About issue and pull request templates - GitHub Docs
Extra: Templates live in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE. Issue forms use YAML to create structured, validated fields. They improve quality but do not restrict who can file.

Front:
During a review, a reviewer proposes an exact code change that the author can apply with one click. Which feature is this?

A) A suggested change, which lets reviewers propose specific edits that the author can commit directly from the review
B) A required status check, which blocks merging until an automated test workflow reports a passing result
C) A saved reply, which inserts reusable comment text but cannot apply an actual code edit to the file
Back:
A) A suggested change, which lets reviewers propose specific edits that the author can commit directly from the review

Suggested changes let reviewers write exact edits in a suggestion block that the author commits with one click.

Reference: Incorporating feedback in your pull request - GitHub Docs
Extra: Suggestions speed small fixes like typos. Multiple suggestions can be batched into a single commit. Status checks and saved replies do not edit code.

Front:
After a review thread's feedback is addressed, what does marking the conversation as resolved do?

A) It permanently deletes the comment thread and all of its replies from the pull request's history
B) It collapses the thread and marks it as handled, helping reviewers track which feedback remains open
C) It immediately merges the pull request into the base branch regardless of other pending review threads
Back:
B) It collapses the thread and marks it as handled, helping reviewers track which feedback remains open

Resolving a conversation collapses it and signals that the feedback has been addressed, keeping reviews organized.

Reference: Commenting on a pull request - GitHub Docs
Extra: Branch protection can require all conversations resolved before merging. Resolving preserves the thread (it is not deleted) and does not merge the PR.

Front:
What is GitHub Actions?

A) A built-in code editor that runs entirely in the browser for making quick edits to repository files online
B) A CI/CD and automation platform that runs workflows triggered by events in a repository
C) A vulnerability scanner that reviews dependencies for known security advisories and raises alerts about them
Back:
B) A CI/CD and automation platform that runs workflows triggered by events in a repository

GitHub Actions automates build, test, and deployment workflows in response to repository events.

Reference: Understanding GitHub Actions - GitHub Docs
Extra: Actions powers CI/CD and general automation (labeling, releases, notifications). Dependency scanning is Dependabot; the browser editor is github.dev.

Front:
Where must a GitHub Actions workflow file be stored to be recognized by a repository?

A) In the .github/workflows directory, using a YAML file that defines the workflow's triggers and jobs
B) In the repository root as a file named actions.json, which GitHub parses at the start of every push event
C) Inside the repository wiki as a Markdown page that GitHub converts into an executable workflow automatically
Back:
A) In the .github/workflows directory, using a YAML file that defines the workflow's triggers and jobs

Workflow definitions are YAML files placed in .github/workflows within the repository.

Reference: About workflows - GitHub Docs
Extra: You can have multiple workflow files, each triggered by different events. YAML defines on (triggers), jobs, and steps.

Front:
In a GitHub Actions workflow, what does the 'on' key define?

A) The specific virtual machine operating system image that each job in the workflow will execute its steps on
B) The list of repository collaborators who are permitted to manually trigger and re-run the workflow's jobs
C) The events that trigger the workflow to run, such as push, pull_request, or a schedule
Back:
C) The events that trigger the workflow to run, such as push, pull_request, or a schedule

The 'on' key specifies which events start the workflow, like push, pull_request, or scheduled cron.

Reference: Events that trigger workflows - GitHub Docs
Extra: The runner OS is set with runs-on, not on. Workflows can respond to many event types, including manual workflow_dispatch.

Front:
What is the difference between GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners in GitHub Actions?

A) GitHub-hosted runners are maintained by GitHub on fresh virtual machines, while self-hosted runners run on infrastructure you manage
B) GitHub-hosted runners can only run public repositories, while self-hosted runners are the sole option available for any private repository
C) GitHub-hosted runners execute jobs sequentially forever, while self-hosted runners are the only runners capable of running jobs in parallel
Back:
A) GitHub-hosted runners are maintained by GitHub on fresh virtual machines, while self-hosted runners run on infrastructure you manage

GitHub provides managed, ephemeral runners; self-hosted runners let you use custom hardware or environments you control.

Reference: About GitHub-hosted runners - GitHub Docs
Extra: Self-hosted runners suit special hardware, private networks, or specific software. Both support private repos and parallel jobs.

Front:
In GitHub Actions, how are jobs, steps, and actions related?

A) A step contains multiple jobs, and each job wraps a single action that runs when the whole workflow is triggered
B) A workflow contains jobs, each job contains steps, and a step can run a command or use a reusable action
C) An action contains jobs, and each job is a single command line that runs directly on the default branch of the repository
Back:
B) A workflow contains jobs, each job contains steps, and a step can run a command or use a reusable action

Workflows hold jobs; jobs hold ordered steps; steps run shell commands or call reusable actions.

Reference: Understanding GitHub Actions - GitHub Docs
Extra: Jobs run in parallel by default and can declare dependencies with 'needs'. Actions are reusable units shared via the Marketplace.

Front:
What is GitHub Copilot?

A) A dependency management service that upgrades outdated libraries and opens pull requests for the new versions automatically
B) A code review bot that enforces branch protection rules and blocks pull requests that fail required status checks
C) An AI pair programmer that suggests code and entire functions in the editor as you type
Back:
C) An AI pair programmer that suggests code and entire functions in the editor as you type

GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant that provides context-aware suggestions inside supported editors.

Reference: What is GitHub Copilot - GitHub Docs
Extra: Copilot suggests code, answers questions via chat, and helps write tests and docs. Dependency updates are Dependabot; review enforcement is branch protection.

Front:
What does GitHub Codespaces provide?

A) A cloud-hosted, configurable development environment that runs in the browser or an editor, backed by a container
B) A static website hosting service that publishes HTML directly from a branch or the /docs folder of a repository
C) A package registry that stores and distributes container images and language packages for a repository's builds
Back:
A) A cloud-hosted, configurable development environment that runs in the browser or an editor, backed by a container

Codespaces spins up ready-to-code cloud dev environments defined by a dev container configuration.

Reference: GitHub Codespaces overview - GitHub Docs
Extra: Codespaces removes 'works on my machine' setup by standardizing environments. Static hosting is Pages; package hosting is Packages.

Front:
What can a user do with the GitHub Mobile app?

A) Compile and run full production builds of any repository directly on the phone without any cloud infrastructure
B) Triage notifications, review and comment on pull requests, and manage issues from a phone or tablet
C) Replace the entire GitHub web interface, including every organization-level billing and enterprise policy setting
Back:
B) Triage notifications, review and comment on pull requests, and manage issues from a phone or tablet

GitHub Mobile lets you manage notifications, issues, and pull requests on the go.

Reference: GitHub Mobile - GitHub Docs
Extra: Mobile is great for staying responsive to reviews and notifications. It complements, but does not fully replace, the web and desktop experiences.

Front:
What is the GitHub Marketplace primarily used for?

A) Selling physical developer hardware and merchandise that GitHub ships directly to purchasing accounts worldwide
B) Hosting the source code of every public repository so that it can be searched and cloned in one central place
C) Discovering and installing apps and actions that extend and integrate with GitHub workflows
Back:
C) Discovering and installing apps and actions that extend and integrate with GitHub workflows

The Marketplace offers GitHub Apps and Actions that add functionality and integrations to your workflows.

Reference: About GitHub Marketplace - GitHub Docs
Extra: Marketplace items include CI tools, code quality apps, and reusable actions. Some are free; others are paid. It extends GitHub, not hosts all code.

Front:
How does GitHub Actions typically enable continuous integration for a project?

A) By automatically building and testing code on each push or pull request and reporting the results as status checks
B) By preventing developers from ever pushing to any branch until an administrator manually reviews and approves the change
C) By encrypting all repository source code at rest so that only authenticated continuous integration servers can read it
Back:
A) By automatically building and testing code on each push or pull request and reporting the results as status checks

CI workflows run builds and tests on events and surface pass/fail results as status checks on pull requests.

Reference: About continuous integration - GitHub Docs
Extra: Required status checks can block merges until CI passes. CI gives fast feedback so problems are caught before merging.

Front:
What is the GitHub CLI (gh)?

A) A browser extension that overlays additional buttons on the GitHub website to speed up navigation between pages
B) A command-line tool that lets you work with issues, pull requests, and other GitHub features from the terminal
C) A replacement for Git itself that stores commit history in a proprietary format incompatible with standard Git clients
Back:
B) A command-line tool that lets you work with issues, pull requests, and other GitHub features from the terminal

The GitHub CLI brings GitHub workflows (issues, PRs, releases, Actions) to the command line.

Reference: About GitHub CLI - GitHub Docs
Extra: gh complements Git, not replaces it. For example, 'gh pr create' opens a pull request without leaving the terminal.

Front:
What does Dependabot version updates do for a repository?

A) It automatically opens pull requests to keep a project's dependencies up to date with newer versions
B) It scans committed code for hardcoded secrets such as API keys and revokes them with the provider automatically
C) It runs the project's unit test suite on every push and blocks merging when any of the tests fail
Back:
A) It automatically opens pull requests to keep a project's dependencies up to date with newer versions

Dependabot version updates monitor dependencies and open PRs to upgrade them on a schedule.

Reference: About Dependabot version updates - GitHub Docs
Extra: Dependabot security updates specifically target vulnerable versions. Secret scanning handles leaked credentials; CI runs tests.

Front:
How should sensitive values like API keys be provided to a GitHub Actions workflow?

A) By hardcoding them directly into the workflow YAML file so that every job step can read them without extra setup
B) By committing them to a plaintext file in the repository root and reading that file at the start of each job
C) By storing them as encrypted repository or organization secrets and referencing them in the workflow
Back:
C) By storing them as encrypted repository or organization secrets and referencing them in the workflow

Encrypted secrets keep credentials out of source code and are injected into workflows at runtime.

Reference: Using secrets in GitHub Actions - GitHub Docs
Extra: Secrets are masked in logs. Never commit credentials to the repo; secret scanning exists precisely because this is a common, dangerous mistake.

Front:
What is the purpose of a dev container (devcontainer.json) configuration used by Codespaces?

A) It records which collaborators are allowed to open a Codespace for the repository and how long each may run
B) It defines the tools, extensions, and settings so every Codespace for the repository starts from a consistent environment
C) It lists the repository's runtime dependencies for Dependabot so that outdated packages can be flagged for updates
Back:
B) It defines the tools, extensions, and settings so every Codespace for the repository starts from a consistent environment

The dev container config specifies the image, tools, and settings so environments are reproducible.

Reference: Introduction to dev containers - GitHub Docs
Extra: Dev containers standardize onboarding so contributors get identical, ready-to-code setups. Dependency tracking is a separate concern handled by Dependabot.

Front:
What is a webhook in the context of GitHub integrations?

A) An HTTP callback that GitHub sends to an external service when a subscribed repository event occurs
B) A protected branch setting that requires all pull requests to pass automated tests before they can be merged
C) A special comment syntax that links an issue to a pull request and closes the issue when the PR merges
Back:
A) An HTTP callback that GitHub sends to an external service when a subscribed repository event occurs

Webhooks deliver event payloads to a configured URL, enabling real-time integrations with external systems.

Reference: About webhooks - GitHub Docs
Extra: Webhooks power chat notifications, CI triggers, and custom automation. They push data out to your endpoint when events happen.

Front:
What are GitHub Projects (the current Projects experience) designed to do?

A) Provide a flexible, spreadsheet-and-board planning tool that organizes issues and pull requests into customizable views
B) Host the project's compiled binaries and release assets so that end users can download specific versions of the software
C) Automatically generate the project's source code from a natural-language description of the desired application
Back:
A) Provide a flexible, spreadsheet-and-board planning tool that organizes issues and pull requests into customizable views

Projects is an adaptable planning tool that connects issues and PRs into tables, boards, and roadmaps.

Reference: About Projects - GitHub Docs
Extra: Projects can live at the user or organization level and span multiple repositories. It plans work; releases distribute binaries.

Front:
In GitHub Projects, what is the difference between the board layout and the table layout for the same items?

A) The board layout permanently deletes closed items, while the table layout is the only layout that retains completed work
B) The board shows items as cards in columns for a kanban-style flow, while the table shows them as sortable, filterable rows
C) The board can only display issues, while the table is the sole layout capable of displaying pull requests in a project
Back:
B) The board shows items as cards in columns for a kanban-style flow, while the table shows them as sortable, filterable rows

Board layout gives a kanban view; table layout gives a spreadsheet-like grid. Both show the same underlying items.

Reference: Changing the layout of a view - GitHub Docs
Extra: Layouts are just different views of one dataset; switching does not delete anything. Both handle issues and PRs.

Front:
How do custom fields enhance a GitHub Project?

A) They restrict which repositories can be linked to the project so that only approved teams may add their issues
B) They let you add metadata such as priority, status, iteration, or effort to items for richer tracking and filtering
C) They automatically write the project's status update text and email it to every stakeholder at the end of each week
Back:
B) They let you add metadata such as priority, status, iteration, or effort to items for richer tracking and filtering

Custom fields (text, number, date, single-select, iteration) add structured data used to group, sort, and filter.

Reference: About custom fields - GitHub Docs
Extra: Single-select and iteration fields are especially useful for status columns and sprint planning. Fields drive views, grouping, and insights.

Front:
A team wants to visualize project items on a timeline against date fields to plan across weeks. Which Projects view fits best?

A) The roadmap layout, which plots items on a timeline using their date or iteration fields for planning across time
B) The board layout, which arranges items into kanban columns but does not place them on a calendar timeline
C) The table layout, which lists items as rows and columns but does not render a horizontal timeline of dates
Back:
A) The roadmap layout, which plots items on a timeline using their date or iteration fields for planning across time

The roadmap layout visualizes items along a timeline based on date and iteration fields.

Reference: Customizing the roadmap layout - GitHub Docs
Extra: Roadmap is ideal for long-range planning and dependencies over time. Board and table lack the timeline visualization.

Front:
How can a GitHub Project reduce manual effort when an issue is closed?

A) By using built-in workflows that automatically update an item's status, for example moving closed issues to Done
B) By requiring a maintainer to manually drag each closed issue into the Done column before it disappears from the board
C) By deleting the closed issue from the repository entirely so it no longer appears in any project or search result
Back:
A) By using built-in workflows that automatically update an item's status, for example moving closed issues to Done

Projects include built-in automation workflows that set status when items are added, closed, or merged.

Reference: Using the built-in automations - GitHub Docs
Extra: Automations reduce manual board maintenance. Closing an issue does not delete it; automation simply updates its project status.

Front:
How do milestones complement GitHub Projects for release tracking?

A) Milestones replace projects entirely by providing the same customizable board and table views with automation
B) Milestones group issues and pull requests toward a dated goal and show a completion percentage for that goal
C) Milestones store encrypted deployment credentials that project automation workflows use to publish a release
Back:
B) Milestones group issues and pull requests toward a dated goal and show a completion percentage for that goal

Milestones aggregate issues/PRs toward a target with a due date and progress bar, useful alongside Projects.

Reference: About milestones - GitHub Docs
Extra: Milestones are repo-scoped goals; Projects are flexible cross-repo planning boards. Teams often use both together.

Front:
How is an existing issue added to a GitHub Project?

A) By forking the issue's repository, which automatically copies all of its open issues into a newly generated project
B) By adding the issue to the project from the issue sidebar or by pasting its URL into the project view
C) By converting the issue into a pull request, which is the only supported way to make it appear inside a project
Back:
B) By adding the issue to the project from the issue sidebar or by pasting its URL into the project view

Issues can be added to a project via the issue's Projects sidebar or by adding their URL in the project.

Reference: Adding items to your project - GitHub Docs
Extra: One issue can belong to multiple projects. Forking copies a repo, not project membership, and issues need not become PRs to be tracked.

Front:
How do labels support triage within a project or repository?

A) They categorize issues and pull requests so teams can filter and prioritize, such as separating bugs from enhancements
B) They assign a fixed due date to each issue and automatically close the issue when that date has finally arrived
C) They grant selected contributors permission to merge pull requests without waiting for any required reviews
Back:
A) They categorize issues and pull requests so teams can filter and prioritize, such as separating bugs from enhancements

Labels classify items for filtering and prioritization during triage; they do not set dates or permissions.

Reference: Managing labels - GitHub Docs
Extra: In Projects you can also use single-select custom fields for status. Labels remain a simple, repo-wide way to triage and filter.

Front:
A project manager wants to see all in-progress items grouped by assignee in a project. Which Projects capability enables this?

A) Filtering and grouping the view by field values, such as grouping by assignee and filtering by a status field
B) Archiving the repository so that only in-progress items remain visible to the whole team in the project board
C) Creating a separate milestone for every assignee so that each person's items appear in their own release goal
Back:
A) Filtering and grouping the view by field values, such as grouping by assignee and filtering by a status field

Project views support filtering by field values and grouping to slice items by assignee, status, or other fields.

Reference: Filtering projects - GitHub Docs
Extra: Saved views let each team member keep a preferred slice. Grouping and filtering are far more flexible than per-assignee milestones.

Front:
How do issues and GitHub Projects relate to each other?

A) An issue is a single trackable work item, while a project organizes many issues and pull requests into planning views
B) A project is a single work item, while an issue is the board that organizes many projects into columns and timelines
C) Issues and projects are interchangeable names for the same feature, and either term can be used without any difference
Back:
A) An issue is a single trackable work item, while a project organizes many issues and pull requests into planning views

Issues represent individual work items; Projects aggregate and organize many items for planning.

Reference: About Projects - GitHub Docs
Extra: Think of issues as the tasks and Projects as the planning surface that arranges those tasks into boards, tables, and roadmaps.

Front:
Why is enabling two-factor authentication (2FA) on a GitHub account important?

A) It automatically encrypts every private repository the account owns so their contents cannot be read by other members
B) It removes the need to ever rotate personal access tokens because the second factor keeps those tokens valid indefinitely
C) It adds a second verification step beyond the password, greatly reducing the risk of account compromise
Back:
C) It adds a second verification step beyond the password, greatly reducing the risk of account compromise

2FA requires a second factor (app code, security key, or passkey) in addition to the password, protecting the account.

Reference: About two-factor authentication - GitHub Docs
Extra: GitHub now mandates 2FA for many contributors. 2FA protects sign-in; it does not encrypt repositories or make tokens permanent.

Front:
What does GitHub secret scanning do?

A) It runs the repository's automated test suite on each pull request and blocks merging when any test fails
B) It detects known secret formats such as API keys and tokens committed to a repository and alerts on them
C) It upgrades outdated dependencies by opening pull requests that bump each package to its latest available version
Back:
B) It detects known secret formats such as API keys and tokens committed to a repository and alerts on them

Secret scanning searches commits for known credential patterns and alerts (and can push protection to block them).

Reference: About secret scanning - GitHub Docs
Extra: Push protection can block a commit containing a secret before it lands. Partners can be notified to revoke leaked credentials automatically.

Front:
What do Dependabot alerts notify a repository about?

A) Dependencies that have known security vulnerabilities, so maintainers can update to a patched version
B) Pull requests that have been open longer than a configured number of days without receiving any review
C) Collaborators who have not enabled two-factor authentication on their accounts within the organization
Back:
A) Dependencies that have known security vulnerabilities, so maintainers can update to a patched version

Dependabot alerts flag dependencies with known vulnerabilities from the advisory database.

Reference: About Dependabot alerts - GitHub Docs
Extra: Alerts can be paired with Dependabot security updates that auto-open fix PRs. They rely on the dependency graph and GitHub Advisory Database.

Front:
What is the purpose of GitHub code scanning (for example with CodeQL)?

A) To analyze source code for security vulnerabilities and coding errors and surface them as alerts
B) To measure how many lines of code each contributor has added so managers can rank developer productivity
C) To automatically format source code according to a style guide every time a commit is pushed to a branch
Back:
A) To analyze source code for security vulnerabilities and coding errors and surface them as alerts

Code scanning statically analyzes code (e.g., with CodeQL) to find security issues and bugs, reporting alerts.

Reference: About code scanning - GitHub Docs
Extra: Code scanning can run on pull requests to catch issues before merge. It analyzes code for flaws, unlike Dependabot which checks dependencies.

Front:
What is the purpose of a repository security advisory?

A) It lets maintainers privately discuss, fix, and then publish details of a vulnerability in their project
B) It automatically deploys a patched release to all users who have installed the affected version of the software
C) It permanently blocks any contributor who reported a vulnerability from opening future issues in the repository
Back:
A) It lets maintainers privately discuss, fix, and then publish details of a vulnerability in their project

Security advisories provide a private space to coordinate a fix and then disclose the vulnerability responsibly.

Reference: About repository security advisories - GitHub Docs
Extra: Advisories support private forks for collaboration and can request CVE IDs. Coordinated disclosure protects users until a fix is available.

Front:
A maintainer wants a collaborator who can manage issues and pull requests, including labeling and closing them, but not push code. Which repository role fits best?

A) The Admin role, which grants full control over the repository including settings, security, and deletion
B) The Triage role, which allows managing issues and pull requests without granting write access to the code
C) The Read role, which allows viewing and cloning the repository but not managing issues or pull requests
Back:
B) The Triage role, which allows managing issues and pull requests without granting write access to the code

Triage lets a user manage issues/PRs (label, assign, close) without push access to the codebase.

Reference: Repository roles for an organization - GitHub Docs
Extra: Repo roles escalate: Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, Admin. Grant the least privilege needed. Read cannot manage issues; Admin is far more than required here.

Front:
How do teams help manage access within a GitHub organization?

A) Teams group members so permissions can be granted to many people at once, and teams can be nested to mirror structure
B) Teams are billing units that determine how many private repositories each individual member is personally allowed to create
C) Teams are automated bots that review pull requests and merge them once all of the required status checks have passed
Back:
A) Teams group members so permissions can be granted to many people at once, and teams can be nested to mirror structure

Teams let organizations assign repository access to groups of members and support nesting for hierarchy.

Reference: About teams - GitHub Docs
Extra: Nested teams inherit parent access, simplifying management. Teams can also be @mentioned and set as code owners. They manage access, not billing.

Front:
What distinguishes an organization owner from an organization member?

A) Owners can only view repositories, while members hold the exclusive ability to change organization-wide security settings
B) Owners and members have identical permissions, and the labels exist purely for display on the organization's people page
C) Owners have full administrative control over the organization, while members have limited access based on their granted roles
Back:
C) Owners have full administrative control over the organization, while members have limited access based on their granted roles

Owners manage all org settings, billing, and members; members get access according to team and repo roles.

Reference: Roles in an organization - GitHub Docs
Extra: Limit the number of owners to reduce risk. Members can be granted specific repository and team permissions without full org control.

Front:
What information does an organization's audit log provide?

A) A record of activity and changes, such as permission updates and repository actions, for review and compliance
B) A ranked list of the most active contributors so administrators can reward the top performers each month
C) A queue of automated dependency update pull requests that are waiting for a maintainer to review and merge
Back:
A) A record of activity and changes, such as permission updates and repository actions, for review and compliance

The audit log records who did what and when across the organization, supporting security and compliance reviews.

Reference: Reviewing the audit log - GitHub Docs
Extra: Audit logs help investigate incidents and demonstrate compliance. They can often be exported or streamed to external systems for retention.

Front:
For authenticating Git operations over HTTPS, what does GitHub recommend instead of using an account password?
